nameStory: The 'large-leaved' part of this plant's name is straightforward – it has notably bigger leaves than its spindle tree relatives. The word 'spindle' comes from the old use of these trees' hard wood for making spindles, the pointed rods used in spinning thread and yarn.
description: Large-leaved spindle is a rounded shrub that grows 8 to 13 feet tall, making it one of the larger members of the spindle tree family. Originally from the Mediterranean and southern Europe, it's occasionally found in New England gardens and landscapes. This shade-loving shrub has a neat, compact growth habit and belongs to the staff-vine family, though it doesn't climb like some of its relatives.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large, broad leaves that are noticeably bigger than other spindle trees, arranged in opposite pairs along the stems. The leaves feel smooth and have a rich green color with fine-toothed edges.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a dense, rounded shrub reaching 8-13 feet tall with multiple stems branching from the base. The overall shape is neat and symmetrical.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, inconspicuous flowers with typically 4-5 petals that appear in small clusters. The flowers are greenish-white and easily overlooked among the foliage.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces distinctive capsule fruits that split open to reveal colorful seeds, typical of spindle trees. The fruits are often pink or red when mature.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth, grayish bark on younger stems that may develop slight ridging with age. The bark feels firm and doesn't peel or flake noticeably.

habitat: In New England, large-leaved spindle is primarily found in cultivated settings like gardens, parks, and landscaped areas rather than growing wild. When planted, it thrives in shaded locations with well-drained soil, as too much direct sunlight can actually kill this shade-dependent species.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge in spring, showing their characteristically large size compared to other spindle trees. Small, greenish flowers appear but are often hidden among the expanding foliage.
seasonality.summer: The large, opposite leaves are at their most prominent, creating dense, rounded foliage masses. This is the best time to appreciate the size difference between this species and other spindles.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may develop fall color before dropping, and any fruit capsules will ripen and split to show colorful seeds. The large leaf size remains obvious even as they change color.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show the opposite branching pattern and smooth bark. Any persistent fruits may remain visible, and the overall rounded branching structure is evident.

funFact: This shade-loving shrub is so sensitive to sunlight that too much direct sun can actually kill it – making it the opposite of most plants that struggle in deep shade but tolerate sun.
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other spindle trees, but the notably larger leaves make identification easier. Remember: 'large-leaved' means exactly that – if the leaves look big for a spindle tree, you've probably found the right one.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'spindle trees,' these plants don't actually spin or climb. The name comes from their historical use – the hard wood was perfect for making spindles used in textile work. This species is quite rare in New England with only 9 recorded observations.
compareHints: Large-leaved spindle stands out from its New England relatives primarily by leaf size – its leaves are significantly larger than the small leaves of winged euonymus or the narrow leaves of other spindle species. Unlike the very common winged euonymus with its distinctive corky wing-like ridges on the stems, large-leaved spindle has smooth bark and focuses its energy on producing those notably large leaves.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Euonymus relatives in New England, winged euonymus is the only one with prominent corky wings on the stems.
Unlike winged euonymus (burning bush) which is deciduous with prominent corky wing-like ridges on stems, Fortune's spindle stays evergreen and has smooth, round stems.
Unlike its notorious relative winged euonymus (burning bush), European spindle lacks the prominent corky 'wings' on its stems and has much less intense fall leaf color.
American wahoo differs from its cousin winged euonymus (burning bush) by lacking the distinctive corky wings on its stems and being much less common.
Among New England's euonymus species, Hamilton's spindle stands out for its four-lobed pink fruits and dangling orange seeds on threads.
Unlike its deciduous relatives like winged euonymus (burning bush) or wahoo, Japanese spindle keeps its leaves year-round.
